solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: the colon clause (missing skull and most of tail) all but defines the word, and 'intact' is its direct opposite, so this is a quick elimination; 'duplicate'/'living' are near-throwaway distractors
S032-01.notes: Missing skull and tail = fragmentary. Intact contradicts; duplicate and living are illogical for a single fossil.

flags: minor: 'outnumbered' is a weak distractor nobody would pick
S032-02.notes: Waverers announced support and the bill passed quickly, so the speech roused them to action (galvanized). Alienated and bewildered go the wrong way.

S032-03.notes: The 'Although long, only a few meters wide and similar in color' sentence explains why the wall is hard to see. D is wrong because the final sentence extends the point and does not reject anything. A misreads 'extremely long'. Facts check out: the wall is roughly 4-9 m wide, and astronauts in low orbit have said it is hard to see.

S032-04.notes: Bears carry carcasses inland, and trees there are rich in marine-type heavy nitrogen and grow faster, so salmon bring ocean nutrients to the trees. A says 'directly from ocean water', which is wrong. C is about bear growth, which is not supported. D reverses the causation. The science matches published riparian 15N studies (e.g., Helfield & Naiman 2001).

flags: minor: the key is the only choice that gives all four numbers needed for a gap comparison, so a test-savvy student can spot it by its form; the choice is also slightly longer
minor: C (only the 50-64 group) is a weak distractor
S032-05.notes: The gap is 45-38=7 points for ages 18-29 and 55-14=41 points for 65+, so D shows a much wider gap among the oldest. A (virtual only) is the main trap, and B (in-person only) shows just half of the gap.

flags: minor: the key closely paraphrases Text 2's last sentence ('inviting the listener to signal...'), so it is close to a lookup
S032-06.notes: The linguists find that the rise is used on certain statements and works as a check that invites listener feedback, which counters the 'uncertainty' claim. B contradicts Text 2. C overreaches from the examples. D is not discussed.

flags: minor: C is the only choice that mentions 17 hours, so matching 'how long' to the longest duration makes this quick
S032-07.notes: The goal is to stress the length of the wait, so C ('up to 17 hours later') fits. A stresses the short 15-minute delay. B and D do not address the wait. This matches Kabadayi & Osvath 2017 (Science).

S032-08.notes: No tailpipe emissions contrasted with high battery-manufacturing energy gives a concession/contrast, so 'Even so'. Therefore, Likewise and In other words don't fit.

flags: minor: A and D also leave 'so well preserved that...' garbled (A has no verb for it, and D repeats 'the people who found' twice), so they are easy to eliminate without spotting the modifier rule
S032-09.notes: The participial phrase 'Excavated from a peat bog' has to modify the body: 'the Tollund Man's body was so well preserved that...' A, C and D are dangling modifiers. The facts are accurate: peat cutters found the body near Silkeborg in 1950 and at first suspected a recent murder.

S032-10.notes: Two independent clauses are joined by the conjunctive adverb 'however', which needs a semicolon before it and a comma after: 'May; however, repairs...' A is a comma splice and the main trap. B is a comma splice with missing punctuation. C is missing the comma after 'however'.
